title: The Story of Ali Cogia, Merchant of Baghdad
paragraphs: In the reign of Haroun-al-Raschid there lived in Baghdad a merchant named Ali Cogia. He had no wife or children and was content with the modest profit his trade brought in. He had spent several years quite happily in the house his father had left him, when three nights in a row he dreamed of an old man who came to him and scolded him for neglecting the duty of a good Muslim by putting off his pilgrimage to Mecca for so long.

The dream troubled Ali Cogia greatly, since he did not want to give up his shop and lose all his customers. For some time he had closed his eyes to the need to make this pilgrimage, and had tried to ease his conscience with extra good works. But the dream felt to him like a direct warning, and he decided not to delay the journey any longer.

First he sold his furniture and the goods in his shop, keeping back only what he could trade with on the road. He sold the shop too, and had no trouble finding a tenant for his house. The one matter he could not settle to his satisfaction was how to keep safe the thousand pieces of gold he wanted to leave behind.

After thinking it over, Ali Cogia came up with a plan that seemed secure. He took a large jar, put the money at the bottom, and filled the rest with olives. He corked the jar tightly, carried it to a friend of his, a merchant like himself, and said:
“My brother, you have probably heard that I leave with a caravan for Mecca in a few days. I’ve come to ask whether you would do me the favor of keeping this jar of olives for me until I return.”
The merchant answered at once, “Here, this is the key to my shop. Take it and put the jar wherever you like. I promise you will find it in the same place when you get back.”

A few days later Ali Cogia climbed onto the camel he had loaded with goods, joined the caravan, and reached Mecca in good time. Like the other pilgrims he visited the sacred Mosque, and when his religious duties were done, he displayed his goods as attractively as he could, hoping to find buyers among the people passing by.
Before long two merchants stopped in front of the display, and after going through the goods, one said to the other:
“If this man were smart, he would take these wares to Cairo. He’d get a much better price there than he is likely to get here.”

Ali Cogia heard this and wasted no time acting on the advice. He packed up his goods, and instead of going back to Baghdad he joined a caravan bound for Cairo. The trip delighted him. He sold nearly everything at once and bought a stock of Egyptian curiosities to sell in Damascus. But the caravan he would have to travel with was not leaving for another six weeks, so he used the wait to see the Pyramids and some of the cities along the Nile.

Now Damascus charmed the good Ali so much that he could hardly bring himself to leave. At last he remembered that he had a home in Baghdad. He planned to go back by way of Aleppo, and after crossing the Euphrates, to follow the Tigris.

But when he reached Mossoul, he had become such good friends with some Persian merchants that they talked him into going with them to their own country, and even as far as India. So it happened that seven years went by after he left Baghdad, and in all that time the friend who had the jar of olives never once thought of him or of it. In fact the matter only crossed his mind a month before Ali Cogia actually came home, when his wife remarked one day that it was a long time since she had eaten olives and she would like some.

“That reminds me,” said the husband, “that before Ali Cogia went to Mecca seven years ago, he left a jar of olives with me. But by now he must surely be dead, and there’s no reason we shouldn’t eat the olives if we like. Give me a light and I’ll go and get them and see how they taste.”

“Husband,” the wife answered, “please, don’t do anything so shameful! Even if seven years have gone by with no word of Ali Cogia, that doesn’t mean he’s dead, and he could return any day. How disgraceful it would be to have to admit that you had betrayed his trust and broken the seal on his jar! Pay no attention to what I said, I don’t really want olives now. And after all this time they’re probably spoiled anyway. I have a feeling that Ali Cogia will come back, and what will he think of you? Let it go, I beg you.”
But the merchant refused to listen to her, sensible as her advice was. He took a light and a dish and went into his shop.
“If you’re going to be so stubborn,” said his wife, “I can’t stop you. But don’t blame me if it turns out badly.”

When the merchant opened the jar, he found the olives on top were rotten. To see whether the ones underneath were in better shape, he shook some out into the dish. As they tumbled out, a few gold pieces tumbled out with them.
The sight of the gold woke all the merchant’s greed. He looked into the jar and saw that the whole bottom was full of gold. Then he put the olives back and went to his wife.
“Wife,” he said as he came into the room, “you were quite right. The olives are rotten, but I’ve closed the jar up so well that Ali Cogia will never know anyone touched it.”
“You would have done better to believe me,” the wife replied. “I hope no harm comes of it.”

These words had no more effect on the merchant than the earlier ones, and he spent the whole night wondering how he could keep the gold if Ali Cogia came back and asked for his jar. Very early the next morning he went out and bought fresh olives. He threw the old ones away, took out the gold and hid it, and filled the jar with the new olives. Then he corked it again and put it back where Ali Cogia had left it.

A month later Ali Cogia came back into Baghdad. His house was still rented out, so he took a room at an inn, and the next day he set out to see his friend the merchant, who welcomed him with open arms and many cries of surprise. After a few minutes of questions, Ali Cogia asked the merchant to give him the jar he had looked after for so long.
“Of course,” said the merchant. “I’m only glad I could be of use to you. Here is the key to my shop. You’ll find the jar where you put it.”

Ali Cogia fetched his jar and carried it to his room at the inn, where he opened it. He pushed his hand down but felt no money, though he was still sure it must be there. So he took some plates and bowls from his traveling kit and emptied the olives out. It was no use. The gold was not there. The poor man was struck dumb with horror. Then he raised his hands and cried, “Can my old friend really have committed such a crime?”

In great haste he went back to the merchant’s house. “My friend,” he cried, “you’ll be surprised to see me again, but I can’t find the thousand pieces of gold I put at the bottom of this jar, under the olives. Perhaps you borrowed them for your business. If so, you are welcome to them. I only ask you to give me a receipt, and you can repay me whenever it suits you.”
The merchant had expected something like this and had his answer ready. “Ali Cogia,” he said, “when you brought me the jar of olives, did I ever touch it?”

“I gave you the key to my shop and you put the jar where you wanted yourself, and didn’t you find it in exactly the same spot and the same condition? If you put gold in it, it must still be there. I know nothing about that; you only told me there were olives. Believe me or not as you please, but I have not laid a finger on the jar.”

Ali Cogia kept trying every means to make the merchant admit the truth. “I love peace,” he said, “and I would deeply regret having to turn to harsh measures. Once more, think of your reputation. I will be in despair if you force me to call in the law.”

“Ali Cogia,” the merchant answered, “you admit that what you left with me was a jar of olives. You came and took it away yourself, and now you say it held a thousand pieces of gold and that I have to hand them over! Did you ever mention any gold before? I didn’t even know there were olives in the jar! You never showed me what was inside. You may as well demand pearls or diamonds while you’re at it. Now go away, please, before a crowd gathers outside my shop.”

By now a number of people had stopped to listen to the quarrel, not just passers-by but the merchants from the neighboring shops, who kept trying to make peace between the two men. But when the merchant had spoken his last words, Ali Cogia decided to lay the whole matter before them, and he told them the whole story. They heard him out, and then asked the merchant what he had to say for himself.

The merchant agreed that he had kept Ali Cogia’s jar in his shop, but he insisted he had never touched it. As for what was inside, he swore that he knew only what Ali Cogia himself had told him, and he called on everyone there to witness the insult he was being made to suffer.
“You’ve brought this on yourself,” said Ali Cogia, seizing him by the arm. “Since you want the law, you will have the law! We’ll see whether you dare to tell your story again in front of the Cadi.”

As a good Muslim, the merchant could not refuse to be taken before a judge, so he accepted the challenge. “Very well,” he told Ali Cogia, “nothing would please me more. We’ll soon see which of us is in the right.”

The two men then appeared before the Cadi, and Ali Cogia told his story once more. The Cadi asked him who his witnesses were. Ali Cogia answered that he had taken no such precaution, since he had thought of the man as a friend and had always found him honest until then.

The merchant for his part held to his version. He offered to swear a solemn oath that he had never stolen the thousand gold pieces, and that he had not even known they were there. The Cadi let him take the oath and declared him innocent.

Ali Cogia was furious at being left with such a loss. He protested against the verdict and announced that he would take his case to the Caliph, Haroun-al-Raschid, in person. The Cadi took no notice of these threats, entirely satisfied that he had done the right thing.

With the judgment given, the merchant went home in triumph, while Ali Cogia returned to his inn to write out a petition to the Caliph. Next morning he stood along the road the Caliph would take after the midday prayer, and held out his petition to the officer who walked ahead of the Caliph. It was this officer’s duty to gather such papers and, once inside the palace, pass them on to his master. There Haroun-al-Raschid went through them carefully.

Ali Cogia knew this custom, so he followed the Caliph into the public hall of the palace and waited to see what would come of it. After a while the officer came out and told him that the Caliph had read his petition and had set a time for hearing him the following morning. The officer also asked for the merchant’s address, so that he could be summoned as well.
That same evening the Caliph went out to walk through the town, as he liked to do, with his grand vizier Giafar and Mesrour, the chief of the eunuchs. All three were in disguise.

As they went down one street, a noise caught the Caliph’s attention. He looked through a doorway that opened onto a courtyard and saw ten or twelve children playing in the moonlight. He hid in a dark corner and watched them.
“Let’s play at being the Cadi,” said the brightest and quickest of the children. “I’ll be the Cadi. Bring Ali Cogia before me, and the merchant who robbed him of the thousand pieces of gold.”
The boy’s words reminded the Caliph of the petition he had read that morning, and he waited, interested to see what the children would do.

The other children welcomed the idea gladly, since they had heard a great deal of talk about the affair, and they quickly agreed on who would play which part. The Cadi sat down solemnly in his seat, and an officer brought in Ali Cogia first, as the plaintiff, and then the merchant, as the defendant.
Ali Cogia bowed low and argued his case point by point. He ended by begging the Cadi not to make him bear so heavy a loss.
When the Cadi had heard him, he turned to the merchant and asked why he had not paid Ali Cogia back the money in question.
The pretend merchant repeated the reasons the real merchant had given the Cadi of Baghdad, and he too offered to swear that he was telling the truth.

“Wait a moment!” said the little Cadi. “Before we get to oaths, I’d like to look at the jar of olives. Ali Cogia,” he went on, “do you have the jar with you?” When he learned that Ali Cogia did not, he said, “Go and fetch it and bring it to me.”

Ali Cogia went off for a moment, then came back and made a show of setting a jar down at the Cadi’s feet. He declared that it was his jar, the one he had given the accused to look after. To be thorough, the Cadi asked the merchant whether he recognized it as the same jar. The merchant’s silence admitted that it was, and the Cadi ordered the jar opened. Ali Cogia made the motion of lifting off a lid, and the little Cadi in turn pretended to peer into a jar.
“What beautiful olives!” he said. “I’d like to taste one.” Pretending to put one in his mouth, he added, “They’re really excellent!
“But,” he went on, “I find it strange that olives seven years old should be as good as that! Send for some olive dealers and let’s hear what they say!”
Two children were brought forward as olive merchants, and the Cadi spoke to them. “Tell me,” he said, “how long can olives be kept and still be pleasant to eat?”
“My lord,” the merchants answered, “no matter how carefully they are kept, olives never last past the third year. They lose their flavour and their color, and are good for nothing but throwing away.”
“If that’s so,” said the little Cadi, “then examine this jar and tell me how long the olives in it have been there.”
The olive merchants made a show of inspecting the olives and tasting them. Then they reported to the Cadi that the olives were fresh and good.
“You’re wrong,” he said. “Ali Cogia states that he put them in this jar seven years ago.”
“My lord,” the olive merchants replied, “we assure you these olives are from this year’s harvest. And if you asked every merchant in Baghdad, you wouldn’t find one who would say otherwise.”

The accused merchant opened his mouth as if to protest, but the Cadi gave him no chance. “Be quiet,” he said. “You are a thief. Take him away and hang him.” With that the game ended, and the children clapped their hands and led the criminal off to be hanged.

Haroun-al-Raschid was astonished at the wisdom of the child, who had judged so wisely the very case he himself was to hear the next day. “Could there be any other verdict?” he asked the grand vizier, who was just as impressed as he was. “I can’t imagine a better judgment.”
“If things really are as we have been told,” the grand vizier answered, “then it seems to me that Your Highness can only follow this boy’s example, both in how he reasoned and in what he concluded.”

“Then mark this house carefully,” said the Caliph, “and bring me the boy tomorrow, so that he can try the case in my presence. Summon the Cadi too, so he can learn his duty from a child. Tell Ali Cogia to bring his jar of olives, and make sure two olive dealers are here.” With that, the Caliph went back to the palace.

Early the next morning the grand vizier returned to the house where they had seen the children at play and asked to see the lady of the house and her children. Three boys came out, and the grand vizier asked which of them had played the Cadi in the game the evening before. The eldest and tallest, turning pale, admitted that it was he. To his mother’s great alarm, the grand vizier said he had strict orders to take him into the Caliph’s presence.

“Does he mean to take my son away from me?” cried the poor woman. But the grand vizier hurried to calm her. He assured her that she would have the boy back within the hour, and that once she knew why he was wanted she would be perfectly content. So she dressed the boy in his best clothes, and the two of them left the house.

When the grand vizier brought the child before the Caliph, the boy was somewhat overawed and confused, and the Caliph set about explaining why he had sent for him. “Come closer, my son,” he said kindly. “I believe it was you who judged the case of Ali Cogia and the merchant last night? I happened to overhear you, and I was very pleased with how you handled it. Today you will see the real Ali Cogia and the real merchant. Sit down right here beside me.”

The Caliph took his seat on the throne with the boy beside him, and the two parties to the case were shown in. One after the other they threw themselves down and touched their foreheads to the carpet at the foot of the throne. When they stood up, the Caliph said, “Now speak. This child will give you justice, and if more is needed, I will see to it myself.”

Ali Cogia and the merchant argued their sides one after the other. But when the merchant offered to swear the same oath he had sworn before the Cadi, the child stopped him and said that first he must see the jar of olives.

At this, Ali Cogia brought the jar to the Caliph and took off the cover. The Caliph picked out an olive, tasted it, and told the expert merchants to do the same. They declared the olives good, and from this year’s crop. The boy told them that Ali Cogia said he had put the olives in the jar seven years earlier, and they gave the same answer the children had given.

By now the accused merchant could see that he was certain to be condemned, and he tried to offer some excuse in his defense. The boy had too much sense to order him hanged. He looked at the Caliph and said, “Commander of the Faithful, this is no game now. It is for Your Highness to sentence him to death, not for me.”

Then the Caliph, convinced that the man was a thief, ordered him taken away and hanged. This was done, but not before the man had confessed his guilt and told where he had hidden Ali Cogia’s money. The Caliph told the Cadi to go and learn how to dispense justice from a child, and he sent the boy home with a purse of a hundred pieces of gold as a sign of his favor.
